description.narrative: FORT aims to strengthen FOs as drivers of inclusive and resilient rural transformation in Uganda’s remote and highland farming systems by improving FO governance, institutional capacity, lobby and advocacy and business performance so they can effectively deliver quality services to members and participate competitively in agricultural value chains. Through enterprise development, market and financial linkages, and capacity strengthening, it will enhance collective action, increase the production and profitability of smallholder farmer households and FO-led enterprises, and improve farmers’ access to quality inputs, finance, markets, and information. The project applies the EFFORT (Empowered Farmers and Farmer Organisations for Resilience and Transformation) approach, which empowers smallholder farmers to take greater control of their development by strengthening their voice, participation, and decision-making influence within farmer organisations through participatory planning, collective learning, and farmer-led action which enhances ownership and sustainability. Ultimately, the project contributes to improved household incomes, stronger resilience to climate and economic shocks, and more inclusive participation of women and youth in rural economies.

The FORT project is an EKN-funded food security project implemented by a consortium led by Agriterra and complemented by Wageningen Social and Economic Research (WSER) and the Uganda Cooperative Alliance (UCA). It has a lifespan of 5 years, starting in November 2024 and ending in October 2029. The project aims to address the structural challenges faced by Uganda's smallholder farmers (SHFs), by supporting sustainable agricultural productivity, increase incomes, and strengthen resilience against climate change and market vulnerabilities by helping SHFs organize and gain access to quality inputs, financial services, and markets. It also helps to strengthen farmers' organizations (FOs), especially less developed or established ones, by making them more transparent, democratic, and accountable to their farmer members. The target is to reach 200,000 farmer households by the support of 180 informal FOs, and 120 formal FOs.

The target group of the FORT program are 200,000 SHFs affiliated with formal and informal Farmers’ Organisations. The three main types of FOs are (1) national organisations, (2) formal cooperatives and SACCOs and (3) informal farmer groups. FORT will work with formal cooperatives and SACCOs to create a bridge to establish connections with informal farmer groups and remote SHFs.

title.narrative: SHFs have increased production, productivity and profitability

description.narrative: SSFPs are Small Scale Food Producers also referred to as smallholder farmers in FORT's context. The indicator tracks the count of farmers whose yield gap has reduced in comparison to the baseline/previous year. The yield gap is the difference between the maximum yield a crop could produce under ideal conditions (potential yield) e.g., using best practices, the right seeds, optimal input use, etc., and the actual yield farmers achieve in their fields. The baseline is the average actual crop yield of targeted farmers before being reached by the NL-supported intervention. Farmers need to have a yield increase of at least 20% to be counted for. Yield data will be disaggregated by crop type (maize, beans, cooking bananas, potato and coffee). The average yield increase will also be reported per crop.

title.narrative: # of SSFPs (disaggregated for male/female) who progressively decrease the yield gap

description.narrative: SSFPs are Small Scale Food Producers also referred to as smallholder farmers in FORT's context. This indicator measures the count of smallholder farmers experiencing reduced vulnerability due to diversified income sources, climate-smart practices, and improved access and utilisation of services including financial services, inputs and markets. It looks at the ability of SHF to mitigate, withstand and recover from economic and climatic shocks and stresses that could disrupt their means of making a living, like; natural disasters, economic downturns, by having diverse income sources, access to necessary resources, and the capacity to adapt to changing circumstances. It looks at risk management strategies , resilience capacities of SHFs and support interventions from FOs that strengthen any or a combination of the 6 capitals ie human, natural, physical, financial, social and political capital.
